--- number-offset: 1 --- # Data Structures in Python {#sec-ch02} Data is the recorded outcome of scientific measurement. Each value captures one observation about one entity: a student's age, the faculty they belong to, the hours they slept during a semester, or their response to a Likert questionnaire item. Before conducting any statistical analysis, a researcher must clarify what each value signifies, what level of measurement generated it, and how the data is organized in computer memory. These foundations determine which summary statistics, visualizations, and inferential models are scientifically valid. Research data rarely arrives in a single pristine file. In Elaf's wellbeing study, the online survey software generated an Excel export (`wellbeing_raw.xlsx`), the university registrar exported semester records as CSV files (`semesters.csv`), and a collaborator from a previous pilot study stored historical records in SPSS (`wellbeing.sav`). Before analyzing these heterogeneous sources, we need to understand how Python organizes data in memory. Python provides specialized structures tailored for data science: **lists** and **NumPy arrays** for basic sequences, **Pandas Series** for single measurement variables, **Categorical Series** for discrete groups, and **DataFrames** for rectangular tables of cases. This chapter introduces these structures, demonstrates how to import files from every common format, and shows how to generate an automated codebook linking every column to its underlying survey question. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## By the end of this chapter you will be able to - Conceptualize data as a rectangular matrix of cases and variables, and identify the unit of analysis. - Create Pandas Series, perform vectorized arithmetic, and filter observations with boolean indexing. - Manage categorical and ordinal measurements using Pandas `Categorical` types. - Construct, inspect, and slice two-dimensional DataFrames using `.loc` and `.iloc`. - Understand dictionaries and 2D matrices when encountered in statistical output. - Import real-world data from CSV, Excel (`.xlsx`), and SPSS (`.sav`) files, preserving survey question labels. - Build an automated codebook that documents variable definitions and measurement scales. - Map familiar SPSS and Excel procedures to Python idioms, and debug common Python error tracebacks. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"} **Teaching & Practice:** [Interactive Lecture Slides](../slides/02-data-structures.html) · [Browser Playground Exercises](../playground/chapter02.html) ::: ## Data as measurement Almost all empirical research data can be conceptualized as a rectangular grid: each row represents a **case** (or observation), and each column represents a **variable**. A case is the individual unit under observation—a student, a patient, an experimental plot, or an institution. A variable is a measured property recorded across all cases, such as chronological age, anxiety score, or study hours. Every cell in the grid contains a single value representing the measurement of that variable for that specific case. This structure, known as the **data matrix**, forms the backbone of statistical modeling. What constitutes a case depends on the research design, defining the **unit of analysis**. Elaf's wellbeing study involves multiple units of analysis across different tables. In the `students` table, each row represents an individual student ($N = 600$). In the `semesters` table, however, each row represents a single student in a specific academic semester, meaning each student appears up to four times: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} semesters.head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
student_id semester gpa sleep_hours study_hours exercise_days caffeine_mg supervisor_meetings wellbeing
0 S0001 1 3.02 7.2 26.0 5.0 130.0 0 74
1 S0001 2 3.27 8.4 17.0 3.0 80.0 1 69
2 S0001 3 3.17 7.8 25.0 7.0 105.0 3 71
3 S0001 4 3.00 7.2 28.0 4.0 145.0 2 74
4 S0002 1 3.25 6.4 32.0 2.0 210.0 3 60
``` ::: ::: The first four rows all correspond to student `S0001`, documenting their trajectory across semesters 1 through 4. Confusing the unit of analysis is one of the most frequent errors in quantitative research. A demographic question concerning baseline enrollment must count each student exactly once. Conversely, an inquiry into GPA trajectories across time requires repeated-measures observations, coupled with statistical techniques that account for within-subject dependency (@sec-ch10). In @sec-ch05, we explore how research hypotheses dictate the appropriate unit of analysis. ## Variables and their values In Python's data science ecosystem, a single variable's values are held in a **Pandas Series** (or a NumPy 1D array). A Series is an indexed, one-dimensional array capable of holding numbers, text, or boolean flags: ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} sleep = pd.Series([6.5, 7.0, 5.5, 8.0, 6.0]) sleep ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0 6.5 1 7.0 2 5.5 3 8.0 4 6.0 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: A Series enforces a single homogeneous data type (`dtype`). If you inadvertently mix numbers with text, Pandas converts the entire Series to an `object` (or string) dtype to accommodate the text: ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} mixed = pd.Series([6.5, "seven", 5.5]) mixed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0 6.5 1 seven 2 5.5 dtype: object ``` ::: ::: Notice that the numbers `6.5` and `5.5` have become text strings. They can no longer be averaged or plotted numerically. This behavior is vital to understand: if a single survey respondent types `"seven"` or `"N/A"` into a numeric field in a web form, the entire column imports into Python as text. We will encounter this exact issue when inspecting the raw Excel export later in this chapter. ### Operations on a whole Series (Vectorization) A defining strength of Pandas is **vectorization**: mathematical and logical operations apply across every value in the collection simultaneously, without needing explicit `for` loops. Converting sleep durations from hours to minutes requires a single multiplication: ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} sleep * 60 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 0 390.0 1 420.0 2 330.0 3 480.0 4 360.0 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Logical comparisons work identically, generating a boolean Series containing `True` or `False` for each entry. For example, identifying nights falling short of the clinical recommendation of 7 hours: ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} sleep < 7 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0 True 1 False 2 True 3 False 4 True dtype: bool ``` ::: ::: Because Python evaluates `True` as 1 and `False` as 0 in numerical contexts, calling `.sum()` counts the qualifying nights, and `.mean()` calculates their proportion: ::: {.cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Count of short nights:", (sleep < 7).sum()) print("Proportion of short nights:", (sleep < 7).mean()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Count of short nights: 3 Proportion of short nights: 0.6 ``` ::: ::: Three of the five nights (60%) were short. This vectorized code operates at identical speed whether analyzing 5 observations or 500,000 observations. ### Selecting values Python uses **0-based indexing**: the first element resides at position `0`, the second at position `1`, and so on. Think of an index as the offset or distance from the start of the array. To select values by positional integer index in a Pandas Series, use `.iloc[]`: ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("First night:", sleep.iloc[0]) print("First and third nights:\n", sleep.iloc[[0, 2]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` First night: 6.5 First and third nights: 0 6.5 2 5.5 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Values can also be extracted using a boolean condition inside square brackets. Pandas filters the Series, retaining only observations where the condition evaluates to `True`: ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} sleep[sleep < 7] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 0 6.5 2 5.5 4 6.0 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: This syntax, termed **boolean indexing** (or logical filtering), reads naturally: *"give me the elements of sleep where sleep is less than 7."* It is one of the most widely used idioms in quantitative Python. ### Changing values Placing an indexed selection on the left side of the assignment operator updates the underlying data. If a participant later clarifies that their second night was 7.5 hours rather than 7.0: ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} sleep.iloc[1] = 7.5 sleep ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 0 6.5 1 7.5 2 5.5 3 8.0 4 6.0 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ## Categories (Categorical Data) Research datasets frequently contain qualitative categories: faculty division, experimental arm, gender identity, or Likert response levels. Pandas represents categorical variables using the specialized `category` dtype (similar to factors in R or value labels in SPSS). A categorical Series displays text labels but stores them internally as compact integers mapped to a defined list of **categories**: ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} faculty = pd.Series( ["Education", "Humanities", "Education", "Health Sciences"], dtype="category" ) print(faculty) print("Categories:", faculty.cat.categories) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 Education 1 Humanities 2 Education 3 Health Sciences dtype: category Categories (3, object): ['Education', 'Health Sciences', 'Humanities'] Categories: Index(['Education', 'Health Sciences', 'Humanities'], dtype='object') ``` ::: ::: By default, categories are arranged in alphanumeric order. However, when categories possess an intrinsic hierarchy (such as employment intensity or Likert scales), you can define an **ordered category** using `pd.Categorical`: ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} employment = pd.Series( pd.Categorical( ["None", "Full-time job", "Part-time job", "None"], categories=["None", "Part-time job", "Full-time job"], ordered=True ) ) employment.value_counts(sort=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` None 2 Part-time job 1 Full-time job 1 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Specifying explicit category orders ensures that subsequent summary tables and plots display categories logically from lowest to highest rather than alphabetically. ### Levels of measurement and Python types The distinction between continuous numbers and categories is not merely aesthetic; it reflects the underlying mathematical properties of the measurement. Categories without an order (such as faculty or academic discipline) are **nominal**. Categories with a strict ranking but unequal or unquantified intervals (such as Likert scales or employment tiers) are **ordinal**. Measurements with uniform, quantifiable units (such as sleep hours, age, or GPA) are **interval** or **ratio** (numeric). @tbl-measurement-types outlines how each measurement level corresponds to a Python data type. | Measurement Level | Example Variables | Python Data Type | |---|---|---| | Nominal (unordered categories) | Faculty, Gender, Department | `category` (or `object` / `string`) | | Ordinal (ordered categories) | Agreement scale, Education level | `category` (`ordered=True`) | | Interval / Ratio (continuous quantities) | Sleep hours, Age, GPA, Scale sum | `float64`, `int64` | | Binary / Dichotomous | Invited to workshop (Yes/No) | `bool` or two-level `category` | : Levels of measurement and their representation in Python {#tbl-measurement-types} ## A table of cases: The DataFrame Most empirical data is organized as a two-dimensional table where each row represents a case and each column represents a variable. In Python, this table is a Pandas **DataFrame**. Each column is a Series sharing a common index. While each column must have a uniform data type, different columns across the DataFrame can store different types. You can construct a DataFrame manually from a Python dictionary: ::: {.cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot = pd.DataFrame({ "student": ["S1", "S2", "S3", "S4"], "faculty": pd.Categorical(["Education", "Humanities", "Education", "Health Sciences"]), "sleep": [6.5, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0], "invited": [True, False, True, False] }) pilot ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep invited
0 S1 Education 6.5 True
1 S2 Humanities 7.5 False
2 S3 Education 5.5 True
3 S4 Health Sciences 8.0 False
``` ::: ::: The most comprehensive way to inspect a DataFrame's architecture is the `.info()` method, which summarizes column names, non-null counts, and data types: ::: {.cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RangeIndex: 4 entries, 0 to 3 Data columns (total 4 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 student 4 non-null object 1 faculty 4 non-null category 2 sleep 4 non-null float64 3 invited 4 non-null bool dtypes: bool(1), category(1), float64(1), object(1) memory usage: 336.0+ bytes ``` ::: ::: ### Selecting columns and rows To extract a single column as a Series, use square bracket notation with the column name: ::: {.cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot["sleep"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` 0 6.5 1 7.5 2 5.5 3 8.0 Name: sleep, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: To slice rows and columns simultaneously, Pandas provides two primary indexers: 1. `.iloc[row_pos, col_pos]`: selects by **integer position** (0-based offset). 2. `.loc[row_label, col_label]`: selects by **label name** or **boolean mask**. ::: {.cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Select the second row across all columns pilot.iloc[1, :] # Select all rows for two specific columns pilot.loc[:, ["student", "sleep"]] # Filter rows where sleep is under 7 hours pilot.loc[pilot["sleep"] < 7, :] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep invited
0 S1 Education 6.5 True
2 S3 Education 5.5 True
``` ::: ::: The final expression combines a DataFrame with boolean indexing: *"retrieve all columns for rows where sleep is less than 7."* This is Python's direct equivalent of SPSS's *Select Cases* or Excel's *Filter*. ### Adding new columns Assigning an expression to a new column name appends it to the DataFrame: ::: {.cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot["short_sleep"] = pilot["sleep"] < 7 pilot ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep invited short_sleep
0 S1 Education 6.5 True True
1 S2 Humanities 7.5 False False
2 S3 Education 5.5 True True
3 S4 Health Sciences 8.0 False False
``` ::: ::: ### The student wellbeing cohort The `students` dataset bundled in `data2thesis` follows this exact DataFrame architecture across 600 participants: ::: {.cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} students.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RangeIndex: 600 entries, 0 to 599 Data columns (total 14 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 student_id 600 non-null object 1 supervisor_id 600 non-null object 2 age 599 non-null float64 3 gender 600 non-null object 4 faculty 600 non-null object 5 programme 600 non-null object 6 study_mode 600 non-null object 7 employment 293 non-null object 8 has_children 600 non-null object 9 lives_away 600 non-null object 10 financial_worry 562 non-null float64 11 workshop 600 non-null object 12 workshop_sessions 600 non-null int64 13 considering_dropout 600 non-null object dtypes: float64(2), int64(1), object(11) memory usage: 65.8+ KB ``` ::: ::: In this output, `object` indicates text strings, `int64` denotes integers, and `float64` denotes decimal numbers. Columns representing categories, such as `faculty`, can be converted to categorical types whenever discrete factor levels are needed: ::: {.cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} students["faculty"] = students["faculty"].astype("category") students["faculty"].cat.categories ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` Index(['Education', 'Health Sciences', 'Humanities', 'Natural Sciences', 'Social Sciences'], dtype='object') ``` ::: ::: Subsetting with multiple criteria uses Python's bitwise logical operators: `&` (AND) and `|` (OR). In Pandas, each individual condition must be enclosed in parentheses `()` because bitwise operators take precedence over comparison operators (`==`, `>`, `<`): ::: {.cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} hs_phd = students[ (students["faculty"] == "Health Sciences") & (students["programme"] == "PhD") ] print("Health Sciences PhD candidates:", len(hs_phd)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Health Sciences PhD candidates: 44 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Inspecting Data Visually in VS Code In VS Code, opening any DataFrame in the **Interactive Window** or **Data Viewer** provides an interactive spreadsheet grid where you can sort, filter, and inspect columns visually without altering the underlying code. ::: ## Matrices and Dictionaries Beyond Series and DataFrames, two additional data structures frequently appear in quantitative workflows: 2D numerical matrices and dictionaries. ### Matrices and correlation grids A numerical matrix is a two-dimensional grid of homogeneous numbers. Matrices arise naturally as the mathematical output of statistical procedures, such as calculating bivariate correlation coefficients across multiple metrics: ::: {.cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} first_semester = semesters[semesters["semester"] == 1] metric_vars = first_semester[["gpa", "sleep_hours", "study_hours", "wellbeing"]] # Compute bivariate correlation matrix correlations = metric_vars.corr() round(correlations, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ```{=html}
gpa sleep_hours study_hours wellbeing
gpa 1.00 0.25 0.06 0.32
sleep_hours 0.25 1.00 -0.56 0.46
study_hours 0.06 -0.56 1.00 -0.24
wellbeing 0.32 0.46 -0.24 1.00
``` ::: ::: Each variable correlates perfectly with itself ($r = 1.00$) along the main diagonal. Specific pairwise correlations can be extracted using `.loc[row, col]`: ::: {.cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} correlations.loc["sleep_hours", "wellbeing"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` np.float64(0.45630448626446257) ``` ::: ::: ### Dictionaries and statistical results A **dictionary** (`dict`) is Python's fundamental key-value container. It stores named attributes enclosed in curly braces `{}`: ::: {.cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} student = { "id": "S0001", "programme": "Master's", "sleep": [7.2, 8.4, 7.8, 7.2] } student["sleep"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` [7.2, 8.4, 7.8, 7.2] ``` ::: ::: While researchers rarely build complex dictionaries by hand, many Python scientific packages return statistical test results as structured objects or dictionary-like containers. For instance, running a one-sample $t$-test with `scipy.stats` to test whether first-semester students sleep 7 hours on average: ::: {.cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} import scipy.stats as stats result = stats.ttest_1samp(first_semester["sleep_hours"], popmean=7.0, nan_policy="omit") print("t-statistic:", round(result.statistic, 2)) print("p-value:", result.pvalue) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` t-statistic: -12.18 p-value: 1.3317009730817428e-30 ``` ::: ::: The resulting object encapsulates the computed test statistic, degrees of freedom, and $p$-value as named attributes ready for automated reporting in your thesis. ## Importing research data Different software packages store tabular data in distinct binary or text formats. Python provides dedicated reader functions for every standard format, each parsing the input directly into a clean Pandas DataFrame. The sample files below are installed with `data2thesis` and located via `dt.example_file()`: ### CSV files A CSV file (*comma-separated values*) is a plain-text table where commas delimit adjacent columns. Because CSV files are universally supported and human-readable, they represent the gold standard for long-term open science archiving. In Python, CSV files are imported using `pd.read_csv()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = dt.example_file("semesters.csv") semester_data = pd.read_csv(path) semester_data.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}
student_id semester gpa sleep_hours study_hours exercise_days caffeine_mg supervisor_meetings wellbeing
0 S0001 1 3.02 7.2 26.0 5.0 130.0 0 74
1 S0001 2 3.27 8.4 17.0 3.0 80.0 1 69
2 S0001 3 3.17 7.8 25.0 7.0 105.0 3 71
``` ::: ::: In your own thesis project, you will typically point directly to your project's data directory: `pd.read_csv("data/semesters.csv")`. ### Excel spreadsheets Real-world survey platforms frequently export multi-column workbooks (`.xlsx`). Pandas reads modern Excel files via `pd.read_excel()` (powered by the `openpyxl` engine): ::: {.cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw_path = dt.example_file("wellbeing_raw.xlsx") raw_data = pd.read_excel(raw_path) print("Dimensions (rows, columns):", raw_data.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Dimensions (rows, columns): (615, 64) ``` ::: ::: This file represents an unfiltered export from the wellbeing survey. The `.shape` property indicates `r raw_data.shape[0]` rows and `r raw_data.shape[1]` columns. Let's inspect the first few entries across the initial six columns: ::: {.cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw_data.iloc[:5, :6] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}
Response ID Q1_Student ID Q2_Age Q3_Gender Q4_Faculty Q5_Programme
0 R0001 TEST 99.0 Female NaN NaN
1 R0002 test NaN NaN NaN NaN
2 R0003 TEST2 30.0 Male NaN NaN
3 R0004 S0191 27.0 male Humanities Masters
4 R0005 S0015 30.0 Male Health Sciences Master's
``` ::: ::: Notice the irregularities typical of real-world research data: test records (`TEST`), unstandardized text variations (`Male`, `male`), and arbitrary missing value codes (`99` for missing age). In @sec-ch03, we walk through systematic cleaning pipelines to sanitize this raw export. If an Excel workbook contains multiple worksheets, you can target a specific sheet using the `sheet_name` argument (e.g., `pd.read_excel("study.xlsx", sheet_name="Semester 2")`). ### SPSS data files Quantitative social scientists frequently receive archives from colleagues formatted as SPSS files (`.sav`). The `pyreadstat` package enables Python to read `.sav` files while preserving variable metadata and response value labels: ::: {.cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pyreadstat spss_path = dt.example_file("wellbeing.sav") spss_df, meta = pyreadstat.read_sav(spss_path) spss_df.loc[:2, ["student_id", "gender", "faculty", "stress_1"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}
student_id gender faculty stress_1
0 S0001 1.0 2.0 3.0
1 S0002 1.0 1.0 4.0
2 S0003 2.0 1.0 4.0
``` ::: ::: SPSS files store underlying survey questions as variable labels. `pyreadstat` extracts these labels into the `meta` object: ::: {.cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Question text for stress_1:", meta.column_names_to_labels["stress_1"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Question text for stress_1: I feel unable to control important things in my studies. ``` ::: ::: Alternatively, if you wish to import an SPSS file directly with numeric category codes decoded into human-readable text categories, Pandas provides `pd.read_spss()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} spss_labeled = pd.read_spss(spss_path) spss_labeled["faculty"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` faculty Health Sciences 154 Education 148 Social Sciences 116 Humanities 95 Natural Sciences 87 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: This seamless interoperability ensures that years of meticulous labeling in SPSS are instantly accessible inside Python. ## Automated codebook generation In an empirical dataset, a cryptic column header like `stress_1` or a numeric value like `4` is scientifically uninterpretable on its own. It acquires meaning only when accompanied by documentation specifying the original prompt ("I feel unable to control important things in my studies"), the response options (1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree), and missing data conventions. A **codebook** provides this reference, serving as the bridge between participant questionnaires and statistical analysis. Because `pyreadstat` parses embedded SPSS metadata, we can programmatically assemble a comprehensive codebook DataFrame: ::: {.cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} codebook = pd.DataFrame({ "variable": meta.column_names, "label": meta.column_labels, "dtype": [str(spss_df[col].dtype) for col in meta.column_names] }) codebook.head(10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ```{=html}
variable label dtype
0 student_id Student identifier object
1 supervisor_id Supervisor identifier object
2 age Age in years at baseline float64
3 gender Gender float64
4 faculty Faculty float64
5 programme Degree programme float64
6 study_mode Study mode float64
7 employment Paid work alongside study float64
8 has_children Has children float64
9 lives_away Moved away from family to study float64
``` ::: ::: For categorical items, the mapping between underlying integer codes and verbal labels is preserved in `meta.variable_value_labels`: ::: {.cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Value labels for faculty:", meta.variable_value_labels.get("faculty")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value labels for faculty: {1.0: 'Education', 2.0: 'Health Sciences', 3.0: 'Humanities', 4.0: 'Natural Sciences', 5.0: 'Social Sciences'} ``` ::: ::: Exporting this table into an appendix provides an automated, error-free documentation trail for your thesis committee and future secondary analysts. ## Exporting data Once raw data has been cleaned, validated, or transformed, the resulting DataFrame can be exported into standard file formats: ```python # Export to CSV (suppressing automatic integer index column) students.to_csv("students_clean.csv", index=False) # Export to Excel workbook students.to_excel("students_clean.xlsx", index=False) # Export to SPSS system file with pyreadstat import pyreadstat pyreadstat.write_sav(students, "students_clean.sav") ``` Setting `index=False` is essential when saving CSV and Excel files; otherwise, Pandas inserts an unlabelled leading column of row numbers into the file. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Preserve Raw Data Immutability:** Never overwrite primary data files. Save processed datasets under descriptive filenames (e.g., `students_clean.csv`), ensuring that your Python script can recreate the clean data from raw inputs at any time. ## Mapping SPSS and Excel workflows to Python Moving from point-and-click tools to scripted programming involves mapping familiar conceptual operations to Python commands (@tbl-spss). | Analytical Task | SPSS / Excel Procedure | Python / Pandas Idiom | |---|---|---| | Open data file | File > Open > Data | `pd.read_csv()`, `pd.read_excel()`, `pd.read_spss()` | | Variable View (types & labels) | Variable View tab | `df.info()`, `df.dtypes`, `meta.column_names_to_labels` | | Inspect data matrix | Data View / Spreadsheet grid | `df.head()`, VS Code Interactive Data Viewer | | Select cases (filtering) | Data > Select Cases | `df[condition]` or `df.loc[condition, :]` | | Compute variable | Transform > Compute Variable | `df["new_col"] = df["a"] + df["b"]` | | Frequency distribution | Analyze > Descriptive > Frequencies | `df["var"].value_counts()` | | Descriptive statistics | Analyze > Descriptive > Descriptives | `df["var"].describe()`, `df["var"].mean()` | | Export data | File > Save As | `df.to_csv(..., index=False)`, `df.to_excel(...)` | : Conceptual mapping between point-and-click software and Python {#tbl-spss} The paramount advantage of Python is transparency. In Excel or SPSS Data View, manual edits and filter clicks are transient and undocumented. In Python, the input dataset remains untouched while your script provides an indelible, auditable record of every transformation. ## Reading error messages and tracebacks Python tracebacks are diagnostic reports explaining precisely where and why execution halted. When an error occurs, scroll to the final line of the traceback to read the specific exception type and description. Four exceptions account for the vast majority of beginner stumbling blocks: **1. `NameError: name 'slep' is not defined`** A variable name is misspelled, or the code defining it was not executed prior to this line: ::: {.cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(slep) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` NameError: name 'slep' is not defined The **unit of analysis** defines what a single row represents (`students` vs repeated `semesters`). - A **Pandas Series** holds values of a single variable. Operations are vectorized, executing across all elements simultaneously without explicit loops. - Python uses **0-based indexing**. Positional extraction relies on `.iloc[]`, while conditional filtering relies on boolean masks `series[condition]`. - Categories are managed via the Pandas `category` dtype, which supports explicit hierarchical ordering for ordinal scales. - A **DataFrame** is a two-dimensional tabular grid composed of individual Series. Subsetting rows and columns simultaneously is performed with `.loc[rows, cols]`. - Data is imported using `pd.read_csv()`, `pd.read_excel()`, and `pyreadstat.read_sav()`. SPSS survey question labels and value encodings are preserved in metadata. - An automated **codebook** extracts column names, survey prompts, and data types to document study variables systematically. ### Key terms Data matrix, unit of analysis, Pandas Series, vectorization, boolean indexing, 0-based indexing, `.iloc[]`, `.loc[]`, categorical dtype, ordinal scale, DataFrame, correlation matrix, dictionary, CSV, SPSS metadata, codebook, traceback. ## Exercises Work through these exercises in your browser using the [Chapter 2 Playground](../playground/chapter02.html) or download the starter project for VS Code. 1. Create a Series with participant ages: `24, 31, 28, 45, 26`. Use boolean indexing to filter ages over 30, and compute how many participants exceed 30. 2. Construct an ordered Categorical Series from `["Agree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"]` with categories ordered logically from `"Disagree"` to `"Neutral"` to `"Agree"`. Verify the ordering using `.value_counts(sort=False)`. 3. In `students`, use boolean indexing with `&` to count how many participants study part-time (`study_mode == "Part-time"`) AND have dependent children (`children == "Yes"`). 4. Add a boolean column `over_30` to `students` that evaluates to `True` for students older than 30. Check how many missing values exist using `.isna().sum()`. 5. Import `wellbeing.sav` with `pyreadstat` and extract the full survey question text mapped to the variable `support_3`. 6. Contrast the unit of analysis in `students` versus `counselling_visits`. Formulate one distinct research question appropriate for each dataset. ## Further reading - *Python for Data Analysis* (3rd ed.) by Wes McKinney [@mckinney2022]: the authoritative guide to Pandas indexing, Series arithmetic, and data wrangling by the creator of Pandas. - Official documentation for [pandas.pydata.org](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/) and [pyreadstat](https://github.com/Roche/pyreadstat).
